chunks: Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal, from his brother Ahmad ibn al-Hasan, from Amr ibn Sa'id, who said:

The brother of Rumayy instructed Umar that all his wealth was for Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him). Umar said: Rumayy informed me that he placed the will before Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said: 'This is what my brother has bequeathed to you.' So I began reading it to him, and he would say to me: 'Stop,' and say: 'Carry this,' and 'I have gifted you that,' until I reached the end of the will. I looked, and found that he had taken only one-third. He said: 'I ordered you to carry one-third to me, and he gifted me the two-thirds.' I said: 'Should I sell it and carry the proceeds to you?' He said: 'No, from what is easy for you from its produce, do not sell anything.'

key_terms.أَبُو جَعْفَرٍ: Abu Ja'far (Imam al-Baqir or Imam al-Sadiq), referred to with honorific
key_terms.الغَلَّة: Produce, yield, or income from property
key_terms.المَيْسُور: Ease, affordability, or what is readily available

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on an Imam's share of an estate when the deceased bequeaths all his wealth to him?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Istibsar illustrates the Imam's voluntary reduction of his bequest share to two-thirds of the estate, demonstrating his generosity and preference for the heir's benefit over liquidation. It establishes the legal principle that the Imam may accept the usufruct (ghallah) of the property rather than its capital, ensuring the heir retains ownership while providing for the Imam's needs. This specific ruling highlights the flexibility in inheritance laws when the Imam waives his right to the full bequest.
